title: SLA Theory — Competing Models

pts: Krashen's Input Hypothesis argues comprehensible input, slightly beyond current level, is the necessary and sufficient condition for acquisition.
This theory underlies extensive reading and listening (Tier II, Units 31–32) throughout this series.
It remains influential but genuinely contested, particularly its claim that input alone is sufficient without output or interaction.

v: Three reading texts at different levels; a class of learners

items: Choose three short texts on the same topic: one clearly easy, one slightly above the class level, one clearly too hard.
Learners read each for two minutes and mark every word or sentence they do not understand.
Collect the marks. Calculate the approximate percentage of unknown words for each text.
Discuss with colleagues: what does ‘slightly beyond current level’ look like in practice, and could you measure it?
Repeat with three listening clips; learners raise a hand where they lose the meaning.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Results from a Class 9 trial (a fictional class):

lines: Text A: about 1% unknown words. Easy. Boring.
Text B: about 4% unknown words. I can follow and I learnt two words.
Text C: about 15% unknown words. I stopped trying.

blocks.x: Krashen described optimal input as i + 1, one step beyond the learner’s current competence (Krashen 1985). A common criticism is that i and +1 are not defined precisely enough to be tested (McLaughlin 1987). Vocabulary coverage research gives a partial operational answer: Hu and Nation (2000) found that adequate unassisted comprehension of fiction needed about 98% known words. [VERIFY exact coverage figure]

body: Purpose: to illustrate comprehensible input. Content: three steps before a learner, labelled ‘too easy’, ‘i + 1’ and ‘out of reach’. Style: simple. Board version: three chalk steps.

items: Text Inspector (limited free use) or VocabProfilers on Lextutor (free) to profile the vocabulary levels of a text. [VERIFY current free limits]

blocks.x: Learners mark unknown words with a pencil dot and count them.

pts: Long's Interaction Hypothesis argues negotiated interaction, not input alone, drives acquisition — the theory behind Tier II's Unit 30.
This can be read as extending, rather than simply contradicting, Krashen's input-focused account.
The debate between these two positions has shaped decades of subsequent SLA research and pedagogy.

v: A recording or transcript of a pair doing an information-gap task

items: Record two learners doing an information-gap task (Unit 30), such as a spot-the-difference picture.
Transcribe one minute.
Mark negotiation moves: clarification requests, confirmation checks, comprehension checks and recasts.
Note where a learner changed their language after a move, and discuss whether this is evidence of acquisition or only of successful communication.
Compare the moves in a one-way and a two-way gap task.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A transcript extract (written for this book):

lines: A: In my picture the boy has a kite.
B: Kite? What is kite?
A: Kite. You fly it. With a string. Paper.
B: Ah, patang! Yes, in mine he has a kite also. But red colour.
A: Red? Mine is yellow.
Moves: clarification request (What is kite?); modified output (You fly it. With a string.); confirmation check (Red?).

blocks.x: The Interaction Hypothesis holds that negotiation of this kind makes input comprehensible and draws attention to gaps in the learner’s knowledge (Long 1996). It extends Krashen rather than rejecting him: input still matters, but interaction shapes it. Whether a moment of negotiation leads to lasting learning is a harder question, which is why researchers use delayed post-tests (Mackey and Goo 2007).

body: Purpose: to show negotiation of meaning. Content: two speech bubbles with a gap between them; a third bubble with a question mark, then a repaired bubble bridging the gap. Style: clean dialogue diagram. Board version: two faces with bubbles and a question-mark bridge.

items: Audacity (free, open source) for recording and slowing down pair talk.
oTranscribe (free) for transcribing audio in the browser. [VERIFY current availability]

blocks.x: The teacher notes negotiation moves live on a tally sheet while listening to one pair.

pts: Swain's Output Hypothesis argues that producing language, not just receiving it, plays a distinct, necessary role in acquisition.
This underlies this series' emphasis on task-based production (Tier II) alongside extensive input.
Together, Input, Interaction and Output Hypotheses form a loosely complementary, if theoretically distinct, family of accounts.

v: A short text for dictogloss (written for this book)

items: Read a short text twice at normal speed. Learners note key words only.
In pairs, learners reconstruct the text as closely as possible.
Pairs compare with another pair and discuss differences in form.
Show the original. Learners mark differences and say what they noticed they could not say.
With younger learners, use four sentences and allow discussion in the home language.
Support: provide the first word of each sentence.
Challenge: rewrite the text for a different audience.

blocks.x: A dictogloss text (written for this book):

lines: Meera had been waiting at Majestic bus station for an hour when the announcement came. The bus to Mysuru had been cancelled. She decided to take the train instead.
S1: I wrote ‘Meera was waiting’.
S2: I think he said ‘had been waiting’. Because it was before the announcement.
S1: Oh. So both were in the past, but one was longer and earlier.

blocks.x: Swain (1995) proposed that output has a noticing function (learners notice what they cannot say), a hypothesis-testing function (they try out forms) and a metalinguistic function (they talk about language).

body: Purpose: to show Swain’s functions of output. Content: a learner speaking, with three labelled arrows: ‘noticing the gap’, ‘testing a form’, ‘talking about language’. Style: clear, three muted colours. Board version: a stick figure and three arrows with short labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for pairs to write reconstructions and compare versions with ‘suggesting’ mode.

blocks.x: Paper reconstructions displayed on benches for comparison.

body: Swain’s Output Hypothesis came from Canadian immersion programmes in which English-speaking children learned school subjects through French. After years of rich input, their comprehension was close to native-like, but their speaking and writing still showed many grammatical errors (Swain 1985).

pts: Whether Chomsky's Universal Grammar remains accessible to adult L2 learners, as it's argued to be for L1 acquisition, remains genuinely contested.
Some researchers argue full UG access persists; others argue it's unavailable or only partially available after a critical period.
This connects directly to Unit 87's later, fuller treatment of the Critical Period Hypothesis.
points.who: The Universal Grammar access debate in SLA

v: Position cards for three views of UG access

items: Summarize the logical problem: children acquire complex grammar from limited input, so Chomsky proposed an innate Universal Grammar (UG).
Give groups one of three position cards: full, partial or no access.
Groups list evidence that would support their position, then present and challenge each other.
Close by linking to the Critical Period Hypothesis (Unit 87) and the fuller debate in Unit 86.
Trainees interview an early and a late learner of English and compare accounts.
Support: one example of evidence for each position.
Challenge: name a finding that would change your position.

blocks.x: Position cards (written for this book, summarizing the literature):

lines: Full access: Adults can still use UG. Their first language is the starting point, but they can restructure it (Schwartz and Sprouse 1996).
No access (Fundamental Difference): Adults learn in a basically different way from children, using general problem-solving and their first language (Bley-Vroman 1989).
Partial access: Some parts of UG remain available, others do not.
A: If adults have full access, why do so few sound native?
B: Access to grammar is not the same as pronunciation. And they may have less input.

blocks.x: The debate remains unresolved, partly because it is hard to show what a learner knows that could not have come from input or the first language (White 2003).

body: Purpose: to show the UG access debate. Content: three doors, open, ajar and closed, labelled ‘full’, ‘partial’ and ‘no access’, with an adult learner before them. Style: neutral. Board version: three rectangles with different gaps.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for a before-and-after vote on the three positions.

blocks.x: A vote by moving to three corners of the room.

pts: Usage-based theories argue grammar emerges from patterns in language use and exposure, rather than from an innate grammar module.
This offers an alternative to nativist accounts, closer in spirit to the cognitive-linguistics approach in Unit 82.
This theoretical family underlies much of the frequency-based, corpus-informed teaching this series has recommended.
points.who: Usage-based linguistics; Nick Ellis's emergentist SLA research

v: Corpus concordance lines or a collection of short texts

items: Give learners 20 concordance lines for a common pattern, such as It’s not worth…, or collect examples from their own reading.
Learners identify the fixed part and the variable part of the pattern.
They sort the variable slot fillers by meaning.
Learners write three sentences with the pattern about their own lives.
Support: provide ten lines instead of twenty, with the fixed part underlined.
Challenge: find a second, related pattern (It’s worth…) and describe the difference.

lines: It’s not worth waiting for the bus.
It’s not worth arguing about.
It’s not worth the trouble.
S1: So after ‘worth’ we put ‘-ing’, or a noun.
T: Yes. You found the slot and what goes in it. You probably learned it by seeing it many times, not from a rule.

blocks.x: Usage-based theory argues that learners build grammar from repeated experience of form–meaning patterns, beginning with fixed expressions and gradually abstracting schemas, and that frequency strongly shapes what is learned (Ellis 2002). This view is close to the cognitive linguistics of Unit 82, and underlies the corpus-informed teaching of Unit 58.

body: Figure 77.5 From many examples to a pattern

Purpose: to show emergence of a construction. Content: many small sentence strips at the bottom, gradually merging upwards into a single pattern It’s not worth ___ at the top. Style: clean, funnel-shaped. Board version: a funnel with example sentences above and the pattern below.

items: SkELL (free, Sketch Engine for Language Learning) for simple concordances of English examples. [VERIFY current access]
Lextutor (free) concordancer.

blocks.x: Learners collect examples of one pattern from their English textbooks over a week.

pts: Selinker's interlanguage concept, used throughout this series (Units 6, 49), sits alongside these competing acquisition theories as a descriptive framework for the learner's evolving system.
It's compatible with multiple acquisition theories, describing the outcome regardless of the underlying mechanism debate.
This is a useful example of how descriptive and explanatory theories can coexist without full agreement.

v: Three pieces of writing by one learner across a term

items: Collect three pieces of writing by one learner, from the beginning, middle and end of a term.
Choose one feature, such as past tense or article use.
Record every use, correct or not, and describe the rules the learner seems to follow at each point.
Discuss which SLA theory would best explain the changes, and whether the description depends on the theory. Unit 49 treats interlanguage and error analysis at B1–B2.
In a teacher group, each teacher brings one learner’s work and the group compares developmental paths.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A learner’s past tense, three snapshots (written for this book):

lines: June: Yesterday I go to temple. We eat prasadam. (present form for past)
August: Yesterday I went to temple. We eated prasadam. (irregular form learned; -ed over-applied)
October: Yesterday I went to the temple. We ate prasadam. (target forms)

blocks.x: The August form eated looks like going backwards but is evidence of progress: the learner has a rule and is applying it widely. Selinker (1972) called the learner’s system interlanguage. The description works whether the mechanism is input, interaction, output, UG or usage, which is why interlanguage has survived the theoretical disputes.

body: Purpose: to show interlanguage development. Content: a U-shaped line graph of past-tense accuracy across a term, annotated with the three sentences. Style: simple chart. Board version: a U-shaped curve with three labels.

items: Google Sheets (free) for recording and charting feature use over time.

blocks.x: A three-column table in the learner’s portfolio (Unit 42).

points.h: Why No Single Theory Has Won
pts: No single SLA theory has achieved the kind of consensus that would settle these debates definitively.
This reflects genuine scientific complexity, not merely poor research — language acquisition is an extraordinarily hard phenomenon to fully explain.
This uncertainty is itself important context for interpreting confident-sounding pedagogical claims.

v: Five theory summaries; a comparison grid

items: Draw a grid with the five theories as rows and three columns: What is learned? How? What kind of evidence?
Groups complete one row each, using this unit and a reference such as Lightbown and Spada (2021).
Groups present and the class fills the full grid.
Discuss why each kind of evidence favours some theories, then each participant writes one sentence beginning No single theory has won because….
Support: provide a partly completed grid.
Challenge: compare the methods of one supporting and one challenging study.

blocks.x: Part of a completed grid (written for this book):

lines: Input: What: implicit knowledge. How: understanding messages. Evidence: comprehension-based programmes, extensive reading studies.
Usage-based: What: constructions and their frequencies. How: general learning from exposure. Evidence: corpus data, frequency effects in experiments.

blocks.x: Acquisition involves memory, perception, interaction, identity and years of time; a field that has not settled it is not a failed field (Mitchell, Myles and Marsden 2019).

body: Purpose: to show theoretical pluralism. Content: a learner at the centre viewed through five labelled lenses, each showing a different part of the picture (ears, mouth, partner, brain, a pile of texts). Style: clean. Board version: a circle with five arrows and labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared comparison grid.

blocks.x: A chart-paper grid completed by groups in turn.

body: When a presenter says ‘research shows’, ask which research and which theory. Laboratory studies of university students may not transfer directly to a Class 7 government-school classroom, and a good source will say so.

pts: This series' principled eclecticism (Unit 25) reflects this genuine theoretical pluralism — no single theory fully justifies one exclusive method.
Good practice draws on multiple compatible insights rather than committing to one theory as the sole truth.
Staying informed about this ongoing debate, without needing it resolved, is itself a mark of genuine professional literacy.

v: One lesson plan the participant has taught recently

items: Each participant chooses one activity from a recent lesson.
Write how each theory in this unit would justify, modify or reject it.
Revise the activity with a change that at least three theories would agree on.
Teach it and note what changed. This is the principled eclecticism of Unit 25 at a theoretical level.
Pair participants so that each justifies the other’s activity.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An example for a reading lesson (written for this book):

lines: Activity: Read the passage aloud in turn; answer ten questions.
Input view: too little input per learner; add silent reading of a longer text.
Interaction view: no negotiation; add a pair task where each partner has half the information.
Output view: no pushed output; add a short retelling for a partner.
Agreed change: silent reading, then an information-gap pair task and a short retelling.

blocks.x: The revised activity is justified by several theories at once, not by committing to one. Lightbown and Spada (2021) take a similar position: that classroom evidence supports a mix of meaning-focused activity and attention to form.

body: Purpose: to show principled eclecticism grounded in theory. Content: a Venn diagram of three overlapping circles labelled ‘Input’, ‘Interaction’, ‘Output’, with ‘rich, meaningful, noticed language use’ in the centre. Style: clear. Board version: three overlapping circles.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable Venn diagram.

blocks.x: Three overlapping chalk circles on the board.

body: Take the next confident claim you meet about how languages are learned. Identify the theory it assumes, then write in your journal how a supporter of a competing theory would respond.

dek: Unit 77 of 100: Krashen's Input Hypothesis, Long's Interaction Hypothesis, and the Universal Grammar debate — the major, genuinely competing accounts of how L2 acquisition works.

aims.x: This unit opens the deep dives of Part IV with the central question of the field: how does a second language get learned? The book has drawn on several answers, from extensive reading to task-based production, without saying that they compete. Here the competition is made explicit: the Input, Interaction and Output Hypotheses, the Universal Grammar debate, usage-based accounts, and interlanguage as a description that survives them all. The unit ends with what theoretical pluralism means for a teacher on Monday morning.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: summarize Krashen’s Input Hypothesis and the main criticisms of it;
explain how the Interaction Hypothesis extends an input-based account;
describe the functions that Swain attributes to output;
outline the positions in the debate about access to Universal Grammar in adult second language acquisition;
explain the usage-based claim that grammar emerges from experience of patterns;
position interlanguage as a descriptive framework compatible with several theories;
explain why no single theory has won, and justify an activity by more than one theory.

why: Why this matters. This series has drawn on multiple SLA theories without fully unpacking how they compete and disagree. Understanding this is theoretical literacy, not academic trivia.

background.x: Until the late 1960s, second language learning was mostly explained as habit formation, with errors blamed on ‘interference’ from the first language. Chomsky’s (1959) review of Skinner challenged the habit view, and error analysis showed that many learner errors were systematic, developmental forms rather than transfer (Corder 1967; Selinker 1972). SLA emerged to explain those systems.

The first large theory to reach teachers was Stephen Krashen’s Monitor Model, a set of five hypotheses about acquisition and learning, the monitor, natural order, input and the affective filter (Krashen 1982, 1985). Its central claim was that comprehensible input is enough. Much of the following two decades of research can be read as responses to that claim: Michael Long argued that interaction makes input comprehensible and draws attention to gaps (Long 1996); Merrill Swain argued that producing language plays roles that input alone cannot (Swain 1985, 1995); and Richard Schmidt argued that learners must notice features for input to become intake (Schmidt 1990). Alongside these, linguists in the generative tradition asked whether adults still have access to the innate Universal Grammar that Chomsky proposed for children (White 2003), while usage-based researchers argued that no such module is needed (Ellis 2002).

These theories differ on what is learned (rules, constructions or associations), how (through a special language faculty or general learning mechanisms), and what the teacher can do about it (Mitchell, Myles and Marsden 2019; Lightbown and Spada 2021). For teachers in India, the debate has practical weight. Prabhu’s Bangalore project deliberately avoided explicit grammar teaching and relied on meaning-focused tasks, a position close to Krashen’s and still discussed internationally (Prabhu 1987). NCF 2023 recommends rich exposure, meaningful use and the home language as a resource, which can be justified by several of the theories in this unit (NCERT 2023). Knowing which theory justifies which recommendation helps a teacher adapt it sensibly when conditions differ.

items: Theory grid. A completed comparison of five theories showing what each says is learned, how, and on what evidence.
Justification task. One classroom activity analysed through at least three theories, with a revision agreed by more than one.
Interlanguage profile. A description of one learner’s development in one feature over a term, with a note on which theories could explain it.
Critical response. A short response to a published pedagogical claim identifying its theoretical assumptions.
Which theory of acquisition did you absorb in your own teacher training, perhaps without its name?
When your learners understand a lot but produce little, which theory helps you most?
How do you respond to an error like eated? Would your response change after this unit?
Which of the debates in this unit most affects your daily classroom decisions?
How comfortable are you teaching without a settled theory? Why?

terms.def: Language that learners can understand, slightly beyond their current level, which Krashen (1982) argued is the main source of language acquisition.

The proposal that adult second language learning differs fundamentally from child first language acquisition, relying on first-language knowledge and general problem-solving rather than Universal Grammar (Bley-Vroman 1989).
Krashen’s formula for comprehensible input: language slightly beyond the learner’s current level (i), made understandable by context, which he argued drives acquisition (Krashen 1985).
The proposal that conversational interaction, especially negotiation of meaning, promotes acquisition by making input comprehensible and drawing attention to form (Long 1996).
The developing language system of a second language learner, which has its own rules and differs from both the first language and the target language (Selinker 1972).
The interactional work, such as clarification requests and comprehension checks, that speakers do to resolve breakdowns in understanding; it is claimed to help acquisition (Long 1996).
Conscious attention to a feature of the input, such as a verb ending, which is argued to be necessary for it to be learnt (Schmidt 1990).
The claim that producing language, especially when pushed to be precise, helps acquisition by making learners notice gaps, test hypotheses and reflect on form (Swain 1985).
Chomsky’s proposal that humans have innate principles common to all languages, which constrain and guide language acquisition (Chomsky 1965). Its role in second language learning remains debated.

The view that language knowledge is built from the expressions people actually meet and use, through general cognitive abilities such as pattern-finding (Tomasello 2003). It emphasizes frequency, exposure and meaningful use.
